processes.title: kernel_task
processes.oneLiner: The core of macOS itself. It also holds busy apps back on purpose to stop your Mac overheating.
processes.summary: kernel_task represents the macOS kernel: the lowest layer of the system, which manages memory, drivers, disks, networking and scheduling for every other process. It always runs and cannot be quit. Apple notes that one of its jobs is temperature control: when the processor gets too hot, kernel_task makes the CPU less available to processes using it heavily, so a big CPU number here is usually a symptom of heat, not the cause of it. Activity Monitor counts 100% per CPU core, so 400% means roughly four cores' worth.
whyHigh: Your Mac is hot (a warm room, blocked vents, sitting on a bed or lap) and macOS is cooling it down
Another app was working hard just before and heated up the processor
Heavy disk, network or external display activity handled by drivers
Virtual machines or containers (Docker, Parallels, UTM) running in the background
A faulty third-party driver or system extension
whatToDo: Give it a few minutes: once the Mac cools, kernel_task backs off on its own
Check which app was using lots of CPU before kernel_task rose, and quit it if you don't need it
Make sure the vents aren't blocked and the Mac sits on a hard, cool surface
Restart your Mac if it stays high while the Mac is cool and idle
If it keeps happening, remove drivers or system extensions you no longer need, or ask Apple Support for a hardware check
processes.safeToQuitNote: It can't be quit because it is the operating system itself. Its CPU use drops by itself once the Mac cools down.

typical.cpu: 1–10% when idle; much higher while cooling a hot Mac
typical.memory: Often several GB; this includes memory reserved by the kernel and drivers and is normal

keywords: kernel_task using a lot of memory

processes.title: WindowServer
processes.oneLiner: Draws every window, menu and animation you see on screen, and routes your clicks and keystrokes.
processes.summary: WindowServer is the macOS display server. Apps draw their own content, and WindowServer combines it into the final picture on each display, handles moving windows and animations, and sends mouse and keyboard input to the right app. It runs whenever you're logged in, and its activity rises with how much is changing on screen. Some CPU use is completely normal, especially with several or high-resolution displays.
whyHigh: Many open windows, or apps that redraw constantly (animated web pages, video, games)
Several or high-resolution external displays, especially at scaled resolutions
Transparency and motion effects, Stage Manager, or many desktops with live content
Screen recording, screen sharing or video calls capturing the screen
One misbehaving app flooding the screen with updates
whatToDo: Close windows and browser tabs you don't need, especially ones playing video or animation
Quit apps one at a time and watch whether WindowServer drops, to find the trigger
Turn on Reduce transparency and Reduce motion in System Settings > Accessibility > Display
Try your external display at its default resolution, or disconnect it to compare
Restart your Mac if it stays high with only a few windows open
processes.safeToQuitNote: Force quitting WindowServer instantly logs you out and closes all your apps, so unsaved work is lost.

typical.cpu: 2–15% when idle; 20–60% with lots happening on screen
typical.memory: 200 MB – 2 GB; more with several or high-resolution displays

keywords: windowserver using a lot of memory

processes.title: launchd
processes.oneLiner: The first process macOS starts. It launches and supervises nearly every other background process.
processes.summary: launchd is process number 1: the kernel starts it at boot, and it then starts the rest of macOS. It launches background services when they're needed, restarts them if they crash, and runs scheduled jobs. There's one system-wide launchd plus one for each logged-in user, so you may see more than one. It's essential and normally uses almost no CPU.
whyHigh: A background job that keeps crashing and being relaunched over and over
Lots of apps and services starting at once, such as right after login
A third-party login item or launch agent misbehaving
whatToDo: Wait a minute after logging in; startup activity settles quickly
Look for a process that keeps appearing and disappearing in the list; that's usually the real culprit
Review System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions and turn off items you don't need
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: ending the system launchd brings down macOS, and ending your user's launchd logs you out.

processes.title: logd
processes.oneLiner: Collects and stores system log messages, the running diary that macOS and apps keep.
processes.summary: logd is the heart of macOS's unified logging system. Apps and system services constantly write short log messages; logd gathers them, keeps recent ones in memory and saves important ones to disk so problems can be investigated later, for example in the Console app. It's always running and is usually light.
whyHigh: An app or service writing huge numbers of log messages, often because something keeps failing
The Console app or the 'log stream' command showing live logs
A diagnostic report (sysdiagnose) being collected
The first hours after a macOS update
whatToDo: Wait a few minutes; short bursts are normal
Close the Console app if it's streaming live logs
Look for another process that is also busy or keeps crashing: it's often the one causing the log flood
Restart your Mac if it stays high
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS restarts it immediately, so quitting won't fix anything and can lose recent log messages.

processes.title: diagnosticd
processes.oneLiner: Feeds live log messages to tools like the Console app and the 'log stream' command.
processes.summary: diagnosticd is part of macOS's unified logging system. When the Console app, the log command or a developer tool is watching messages live, diagnosticd collects and delivers that stream. Apple notes that live viewing makes logging cost extra CPU. When nothing is watching, it sits mostly idle.
whyHigh: The Console app open and streaming live messages
A 'log stream' command, or a monitoring or security tool reading the live log
Developer tools such as Xcode showing a running app's logs
whatToDo: Close the Console app or stop any 'log stream' command
Quit monitoring or developer tools that read logs, then check again
Restart your Mac if it stays busy with nothing watching the logs
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches when needed; quitting it just interrupts any live log viewing.

processes.title: powerd
processes.oneLiner: Manages sleep, wake, battery and charging, and tracks apps asking to keep the Mac awake.
processes.summary: powerd is the macOS daemon behind your energy settings. It decides when the Mac and display may sleep, tracks battery and charging state, and keeps track of apps that ask the Mac to stay awake (called power assertions). It runs all the time and normally uses very little CPU.
whyHigh: Apps repeatedly asking to keep the Mac awake, then letting it sleep
Frequent sleep and wake cycles, or a device that keeps waking the Mac
Charger or battery changes, sometimes from a faulty cable or adapter
whatToDo: Wait a moment; spikes around sleep and wake are normal
Run 'pmset -g assertions' in Terminal to see which apps are keeping the Mac awake
Unplug and reconnect the charger, or try a different cable
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: sleep, wake and battery management depend on it, and macOS starts it again anyway.

processes.title: distnoted
processes.oneLiner: Passes 'something changed' messages between apps and system services behind the scenes.
processes.summary: distnoted is the distributed notification server. Apps use it to broadcast short internal notices to each other, such as 'the appearance switched to Dark Mode', and distnoted delivers them to every app that's listening. These aren't the notification banners you see on screen. You'll usually see one system copy and one per logged-in user.
whyHigh: An app broadcasting a flood of notices, often stuck in a loop
Many apps launching or changing settings at once
A buggy app, plug-in or menu bar utility
whatToDo: Wait a minute; brief spikes are normal
Quit recently installed or updated apps one at a time to see if it calms down
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it, but apps relying on it can misbehave until you restart, so there's no benefit in quitting it.

processes.title: cfprefsd
processes.oneLiner: Reads and saves the settings (preferences) of every app and of macOS itself.
processes.summary: cfprefsd is the preferences server: whenever an app reads or changes a setting, cfprefsd handles the request and keeps the preference files on disk in sync. There's one system copy plus one per logged-in user. It's critical plumbing and is normally very light.
whyHigh: An app reading or writing its settings in a tight loop
A very large or damaged preference file
Many apps launching together, such as right after login
whatToDo: Wait a minute after login or after opening several apps
Quit recently opened apps one by one to find the one hammering its settings
Restart your Mac
If the same app keeps causing it, update or reinstall that app
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it automatically, but a setting change that was in progress could be lost.

processes.title: UserEventAgent
processes.oneLiner: Reacts to system events like network changes and device connections using Apple's plug-ins.
processes.summary: UserEventAgent loads Apple's system plug-ins that respond to high-level events launchd can't watch directly, such as network changes, devices being connected, or power events, and triggers the right services in response. There's one copy for the system and one per user. It runs constantly and should stay light.
whyHigh: Frequent network or Wi-Fi changes
A dock, hub or Bluetooth device repeatedly connecting and disconnecting
A plug-in reacting to an event over and over
whatToDo: Check whether a dock, hub or loose cable keeps connecting and disconnecting
Turn Wi-Fi off and on, or rejoin a network that keeps dropping
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; some automatic reactions to events may be missed for a moment.

processes.title: loginwindow
processes.oneLiner: Handles logging in and out, the lock screen, and keeps your user session running.
processes.summary: loginwindow shows the login screen, starts your session after you log in, handles the lock screen and the Force Quit window, and manages logging out, restarting and shutting down. It keeps running for your whole session even though you don't see it.
whyHigh: Right after login, while your session and login items start
Fast user switching, or locking and unlocking the screen
An app that blocks logging out or shutting down
whatToDo: Wait a minute after logging in
Turn off login items you don't need in System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Quitting loginwindow immediately logs you out and closes all your apps.

processes.title: Dock
processes.oneLiner: Runs the Dock, plus Mission Control, Spaces (multiple desktops), App Exposé and Hot Corners.
processes.summary: The Dock process draws the Dock and also powers Mission Control, Spaces, App Exposé and Hot Corners. It's always running. If you force quit it, it restarts by itself within a second or two, which is a common, harmless fix when the Dock or Mission Control gets stuck.
whyHigh: Mission Control, Spaces or Dock animations in use
Many apps open with lots of windows
A stuck animation or glitch after waking from sleep or changing displays
whatToDo: Wait a moment after using Mission Control or switching desktops
Force quit Dock; macOS relaunches it immediately and this often clears glitches
Restart your Mac if it keeps happening
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches by itself straight away, so quitting is a safe way to reset a stuck Dock or Mission Control.

processes.title: Finder
processes.oneLiner: The Mac's file browser, which also draws the icons on your desktop.
processes.summary: Finder is the app you use to browse files, and it also draws the icons on your desktop, so it's always running. Activity is normal when opening big folders, copying files, generating previews, or browsing network and cloud drives.
whyHigh: Folders with thousands of files, or lots of images and videos needing previews
Copying, moving or emptying the Trash with many files
Cloud storage (iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive) syncing or updating file badges
Slow or disconnected network drives
Third-party Finder extensions
whatToDo: Let file copies or emptying the Trash finish
Close Finder windows showing huge folders or network drives
Option-right-click the Finder icon in the Dock and choose Relaunch
Turn off Finder extensions you don't need in System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Finder relaunches automatically, but a file copy in progress may be interrupted.
keywords: Finder using a lot of memory

processes.title: SystemUIServer
processes.oneLiner: Hosts some menu bar items and other bits of the system interface.
processes.summary: SystemUIServer is a long-standing macOS process that hosts some menu bar items and related system interface pieces. In recent versions of macOS most of Apple's menu bar icons moved to Control Center, so SystemUIServer usually does very little. If something it shows freezes, quitting it is harmless because it relaunches immediately.
whyHigh: A menu bar item it hosts is stuck or updating constantly
A glitch after waking from sleep or connecting a display
whatToDo: Wait a moment
Force quit it; macOS relaunches it right away
Restart your Mac if it keeps happening
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches immediately; menu bar items may blink out for a second.

processes.title: ControlCenter
processes.oneLiner: Runs Control Center and most of Apple's menu bar icons: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, sound, battery, clock.
processes.summary: ControlCenter powers the Control Center panel and most of Apple's own menu bar items, including Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Sound, Battery, Focus, Now Playing and the clock. It's always running while you're logged in. It usually uses little CPU, although it updates often as battery level, media playback and connections change.
whyHigh: Now Playing or other live modules updating frequently
A glitch after waking from sleep or changing displays
Lots of menu bar items or Control Center modules
whatToDo: Close the Control Center panel if it's open
Force quit ControlCenter; it relaunches immediately and often clears glitches
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches instantly; menu bar icons vanish for a moment and then come back.

processes.title: NotificationCenter
processes.oneLiner: Shows notification banners and the Notification Center panel with its widgets.
processes.summary: NotificationCenter draws notification banners and alerts, and the Notification Center panel that opens when you click the date and time in the menu bar, including its widgets. Delivering notifications behind the scenes is handled by a separate process, usernoted. Seeing it running all the time is normal.
whyHigh: Lots of widgets, especially ones that refresh often
An app sending a flood of notifications
A stuck widget or banner
whatToDo: Remove widgets you don't use (Edit Widgets at the bottom of Notification Center)
Turn off notifications for noisy apps in System Settings > Notifications
Force quit NotificationCenter; it relaunches automatically
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches automatically; banners on screen at that moment will disappear.

processes.title: usernoted
processes.oneLiner: Delivers notifications from apps and the system so they can appear on screen.
processes.summary: usernoted is the Notification Center daemon. It receives notifications from apps and from macOS, applies your notification settings and Focus rules, and stores them so they can be shown as banners and in Notification Center. It runs all the time and is usually very light.
whyHigh: An app sending lots of notifications in a short time
Many apps delivering notifications at once after waking from sleep
A large backlog of stored notifications
whatToDo: Clear old notifications in Notification Center
Turn off or limit notifications for noisy apps in System Settings > Notifications
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; notifications may be delayed for a moment.

processes.title: WindowManager
processes.oneLiner: Powers Stage Manager and related window-management features.
processes.summary: WindowManager is the macOS process behind Stage Manager, which groups your windows and shows recent apps along the side of the screen, along with related window-handling features. It runs even when Stage Manager is off, and is usually light.
whyHigh: Stage Manager in use with many apps and windows
Window animations or a glitch after changing displays
whatToDo: Turn Stage Manager off in Control Center to compare
Force quit WindowManager; macOS relaunches it
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches automatically; window arrangements may briefly reset.

processes.title: WallpaperAgent
processes.oneLiner: Draws your desktop wallpaper, including the moving aerial and dynamic wallpapers.
processes.summary: WallpaperAgent manages your desktop and lock screen wallpaper, with helper extensions for still images and for video-based aerial wallpapers. Moving aerial wallpapers are real video, so they cost more memory and power than a still picture. Users have reported the video extension using a lot of memory at times.
whyHigh: A moving aerial or video wallpaper playing, especially across several displays
Using the same aerial as wallpaper and screen saver
Many desktops (Spaces) with different wallpapers
A memory build-up after long uptime
whatToDo: Switch to a still wallpaper in System Settings > Wallpaper to see if usage drops
Turn on 'Show on all Spaces' in Wallpaper settings so one wallpaper is shared
Force quit WallpaperAgent; macOS relaunches it
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches automatically; your wallpaper may flicker or go blank briefly.

typical.memory: 30–300 MB; can be much more with aerial video wallpapers

processes.title: Quick Look (QuickLookUIService)
processes.oneLiner: Makes file previews and thumbnails, like when you press Space on a file in Finder.
processes.summary: Quick Look is the macOS feature that previews a file when you press the Space bar and draws thumbnails of documents, photos and videos in Finder and Open dialogs. Several processes share the work: QuickLookUIService shows previews, while thumbnail and preview generators read the files in the background. They run on demand and go quiet when you stop browsing.
whyHigh: Browsing folders with lots of photos, videos or PDFs that need thumbnails
Previewing a very large or complex file
A third-party Quick Look plug-in struggling with a file
whatToDo: Wait for thumbnails to finish generating; it's a one-time cost per file
Close the preview window or switch Finder to list view for huge folders
Remove or update third-party Quick Look extensions you don't need
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: They relaunch when needed; an open preview will close.

processes.title: UniversalControl
processes.oneLiner: Lets one keyboard and mouse control nearby Macs and iPads (Universal Control).
processes.summary: UniversalControl powers Universal Control, the Continuity feature that lets you move your pointer and keyboard between a Mac and nearby Macs or iPads signed in to the same Apple Account. It runs in the background so devices can find each other, and it's normally light.
whyHigh: Actively controlling another device, or dragging files between devices
Nearby devices repeatedly connecting and disconnecting
Bluetooth or Wi-Fi problems causing retries
whatToDo: Wait if you're actively using Universal Control
If you don't use it, turn it off in System Settings > Displays > Advanced
Turn Bluetooth and Wi-Fi off and on
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches; any active Universal Control connection will drop.

processes.title: configd
processes.oneLiner: Keeps track of network and system configuration and tells apps when it changes.
processes.summary: configd is the System Configuration daemon. It tracks the current state of things like network interfaces, IP addresses, DNS settings and the computer name, applies changes, and notifies apps when something changes, for example when you switch Wi-Fi networks. It's essential and normally very light.
whyHigh: Network changes happening often: flaky Wi-Fi, VPNs connecting and disconnecting
Many network interfaces from VPNs, virtual machines or docks
A network tool repeatedly changing settings
whatToDo: Check whether Wi-Fi or a VPN keeps dropping and reconnecting
Disconnect VPN or virtual-machine software temporarily to compare
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: networking depends on it, and macOS relaunches it anyway.

processes.title: mDNSResponder
processes.oneLiner: Looks up website addresses (DNS) and finds devices like printers on your network (Bonjour).
processes.summary: mDNSResponder is the system's DNS resolver: every time an app needs to turn a name like apple.com into an address, mDNSResponder does the lookup and caches the answer. It also runs Bonjour, which lets your Mac discover printers, AirPlay speakers and other devices on the local network. It's essential and its activity follows your network use.
whyHigh: Apps making very large numbers of network lookups (browsers, sync tools, ad blockers)
Lots of Bonjour devices on a busy network
VPN or DNS-filtering software changing settings
A network problem causing lookups to retry
whatToDo: Wait a moment; short bursts are normal when browsing or syncing
Quit network-heavy apps one at a time to find the trigger
Temporarily disconnect VPN or DNS filter software to compare
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: internet name lookups stop until macOS relaunches it.

processes.title: opendirectoryd
processes.oneLiner: Looks up user accounts, groups and passwords, locally or from a company directory.
processes.summary: opendirectoryd answers questions like 'who is this user?' and 'is this password correct?' for the rest of macOS. It reads the Mac's local account database and, on work Macs, can also talk to directory services such as Active Directory or LDAP. It's essential and normally quiet.
whyHigh: Logging in, or many apps checking user or group information
A company directory server that is slow or unreachable
Management or security software querying accounts frequently
whatToDo: Wait a minute after login
On a work Mac, check your connection to the company network or VPN
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: logins and permission checks depend on it.

processes.title: coreaudiod
processes.oneLiner: Handles all sound on your Mac: playback, microphones, and audio devices.
processes.summary: coreaudiod is the Core Audio daemon. Every sound your Mac plays or records passes through it, and it manages speakers, headphones, microphones and audio interfaces. It's normal for it to use some CPU while audio is playing, during calls, or when an app keeps an audio device open.
whyHigh: Audio or video playing, or a video call in progress
An app keeping the microphone or speakers open in the background
Third-party audio drivers or virtual audio devices (from meeting, recording or audio-routing apps)
Bluetooth headphones switching profiles
whatToDo: Pause playback and end calls, then check again
Quit apps that might be holding audio open, such as meeting or recording apps
Remove audio software you no longer use
Force quit coreaudiod if sound is stuck or crackling; macOS relaunches it within seconds
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it within seconds; sound cuts out briefly and some apps may need restarting to get audio back.

typical.cpu: 0–2% when silent; 2–15% while playing or recording

processes.title: hidd
processes.oneLiner: Processes input from keyboards, mice, trackpads and other human interface devices.
processes.summary: hidd is the userland part of macOS's HID (Human Interface Device) system. It processes events from keyboards, mice, trackpads and similar devices before they reach the rest of the system. It uses a little CPU whenever you type or move the pointer.
whyHigh: Rapid mouse or trackpad movement, especially with high-polling gaming mice
A faulty device or cable sending constant events
Third-party input utilities remapping keys or buttons
whatToDo: Unplug external input devices one at a time to find a faulty one
Quit input utilities (key remappers, mouse software) to compare
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: keyboard and mouse input depend on it.

processes.title: bluetoothd
processes.oneLiner: Runs Bluetooth: connects headphones, keyboards, mice and helps nearby Apple devices find each other.
processes.summary: bluetoothd is the Bluetooth daemon. It manages pairing and connections for AirPods, headphones, keyboards, mice, game controllers and more. BTLEServer handles Bluetooth Low Energy, which Continuity features like Handoff and Unlock with Apple Watch also use. Some activity is constant because the Mac listens for nearby devices.
whyHigh: Many Bluetooth devices connected, or audio streaming to headphones
A device repeatedly connecting and disconnecting
Continuity features (Handoff, AirDrop, Universal Control) searching for nearby devices
Interference or a failing device
whatToDo: Disconnect Bluetooth devices you aren't using
Remove and re-pair a device that keeps dropping
Turn Bluetooth off and on in Control Center
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it, but all Bluetooth devices disconnect, including a Bluetooth keyboard or mouse.

processes.title: airportd
processes.oneLiner: Manages your Mac's Wi-Fi: scanning, joining networks and staying connected.
processes.summary: airportd is the Wi-Fi daemon. It scans for networks, joins and roams between them, and keeps the wireless connection healthy. The name comes from Apple's old AirPort Wi-Fi brand. It's always running when Wi-Fi is on.
whyHigh: Frequent scanning because the signal is weak or the network keeps dropping
Many nearby networks, or roaming between access points
AirDrop, AirPlay or other wireless features in use
Wi-Fi diagnostics or monitoring tools
whatToDo: Move closer to the router or restart the router
Turn Wi-Fi off and on in Control Center
Forget and rejoin a network that keeps dropping
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: Wi-Fi drops until macOS relaunches it.

processes.title: WiFiAgent
processes.oneLiner: Handles Wi-Fi tasks for you, like login pages and network prompts, on behalf of airportd.
processes.summary: WiFiAgent is the per-user Wi-Fi helper. It performs Wi-Fi tasks for the airportd daemon that need to happen in your login session, such as showing network prompts and captive portal login pages at hotels or cafés. It's normally idle.
whyHigh: Joining a network with a login page
Wi-Fi repeatedly connecting and disconnecting
whatToDo: Finish or close any Wi-Fi login page
Turn Wi-Fi off and on
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches; Wi-Fi prompts may not appear until it does.

processes.title: thermalmonitord
processes.oneLiner: Watches your Mac's temperature and helps decide when the system needs to slow down to cool off.
processes.summary: thermalmonitord is a macOS daemon involved in thermal management: it keeps track of temperature and thermal pressure so the system and apps can adjust when the Mac gets hot. Apple doesn't document it in detail, but it's a normal part of macOS and is usually very light. Heavy activity here usually means the Mac is warm, not that something is wrong with the process.
whyHigh: The Mac is hot from heavy work, a warm room or blocked vents
Rapid changes in load, such as games or video exports
whatToDo: Let the Mac cool: quit heavy apps and keep vents clear
Use the Mac on a hard surface rather than a bed or lap
Restart your Mac if it stays busy while cool and idle
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: it's part of how macOS protects your Mac from overheating.

processes.title: corebrightnessd
processes.oneLiner: Manages Night Shift and related display brightness and colour adjustments.
processes.summary: corebrightnessd is the daemon Apple documents as managing Night Shift, the feature that warms the screen's colours in the evening. It's also involved in display brightness and colour adjustments. It runs in the background and is normally very light.
whyHigh: Night Shift or auto-brightness changing often
Connecting or disconnecting displays
Third-party brightness or colour utilities
whatToDo: Quit third-party display utilities to compare
Toggle Night Shift in System Settings > Displays
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; Night Shift and brightness may glitch briefly.

processes.title: sysmond
processes.oneLiner: The system monitor daemon that supplies process statistics to tools like Activity Monitor.
processes.summary: sysmond is Apple's system monitor daemon. It gathers statistics about running processes, such as CPU and memory use, for monitoring tools including Activity Monitor. It's busier when such tools are open and refreshing often, which is expected.
whyHigh: Activity Monitor or other monitoring tools open and refreshing frequently
A very large number of running processes
whatToDo: Close monitoring tools you aren't using, or lower their update frequency
Restart your Mac if it stays busy with no monitor open
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches when needed; monitoring tools may briefly show no data.

processes.title: symptomsd
processes.oneLiner: Part of Apple's Symptoms framework, which watches network conditions to help diagnose problems.
processes.summary: symptomsd provides services for Apple's Symptoms framework, which keeps an eye on network behaviour and conditions so macOS can detect and work around connection problems. Apple documents it only briefly. It runs in the background and is normally light.
whyHigh: Lots of network activity or an unstable connection
Network changes such as switching Wi-Fi networks or VPNs
whatToDo: Check whether your connection keeps dropping
Temporarily disconnect VPN software to compare
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; there's no benefit in quitting it.

processes.title: ReportCrash
processes.oneLiner: Writes a crash report whenever an app or background process crashes.
processes.summary: ReportCrash runs automatically when something crashes. It examines the crashed process and saves a crash report, which developers (and Apple, if you share analytics) use to fix bugs. Reports are saved in Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports and can be viewed in the Console app. Seeing it busy means something is crashing, often repeatedly.
whyHigh: An app or background service crashing over and over
A large app crashing, which takes longer to analyse
Several crashes at once after an update
whatToDo: Open the Console app and look under Crash Reports to see which app is crashing
Update or reinstall that app, or quit it if it's not needed
Restart your Mac
If an Apple process keeps crashing, install the latest macOS update
processes.safeToQuitNote: Quitting stops the current report but doesn't fix the crashing app; it will run again at the next crash.

processes.title: spindump
processes.oneLiner: Records what an unresponsive app was doing, usually when it hangs or is force quit.
processes.summary: spindump samples what every process on the Mac is doing for a short time. macOS runs it automatically when an app stops responding or is force quit, so the report can help explain the hang. It can use a lot of CPU for a few seconds, then exits. Reports are stored in /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports.
whyHigh: An app is hanging (spinning beach ball) or you just force quit one
Many apps hanging at once, such as under heavy memory pressure
A diagnostic report being collected
whatToDo: Wait a few seconds; it finishes quickly
Find which app hung or was force quit, and update or restart it
If many apps hang, check memory pressure and close heavy apps
Restart your Mac if hangs keep happening
processes.safeToQuitNote: Quitting just cancels the current report; it doesn't affect your apps.

processes.title: kernelmanagerd
processes.oneLiner: Loads kernel extensions and starts driver extensions for the macOS kernel.
processes.summary: kernelmanagerd is the kernel extension server. It handles requests to load kernel extensions (kexts) and launches driver extensions, and it prepares newly installed kexts so they can load after a restart. It's mostly idle except during startup or when drivers are installed or removed.
whyHigh: Installing or updating software that includes drivers or kernel extensions
Startup, while drivers are loaded
A third-party driver being repeatedly loaded
whatToDo: Let any software installation finish
Restart your Mac if an installer asked you to
Remove third-party drivers you no longer need using their own uninstallers
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: loading drivers depends on it.

processes.title: sysextd
processes.oneLiner: Manages system extensions, the modern replacement for kernel extensions (VPNs, security tools, drivers).
processes.summary: sysextd helps install, approve, update and remove system extensions. These are modern add-ons used by VPN apps, firewalls, antivirus tools and some drivers that run outside the kernel for safety. It starts on demand and is normally quiet.
whyHigh: Installing or updating a VPN, firewall, security tool or driver
An extension waiting for your approval in System Settings
whatToDo: Approve or deny pending extensions in System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions
Let installations finish
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches when needed; an extension install in progress might fail.

processes.title: lsd
processes.oneLiner: Launch Services: knows which apps are installed and which app opens which file type.
processes.summary: lsd provides Launch Services, the part of macOS that keeps a database of installed apps, which app opens which kind of file or link, and app icons and identities. Apple says it must not be terminated. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with drugs; it's simply short for Launch Services daemon.
whyHigh: Installing, updating or deleting apps
Connecting a drive that contains apps
Rebuilding the Launch Services database
whatToDo: Wait for app installs and updates to finish
Eject drives full of apps you aren't using
Restart your Mac if it stays high
processes.safeToQuitNote: Apple says it must not be terminated; opening apps and files depends on it.

processes.title: coreservicesd
processes.oneLiner: Provides low-level services that Finder and apps rely on to open, launch and track things.
processes.summary: coreservicesd provides various services for macOS's CoreServices frameworks, which apps and Finder use for tasks like launching apps and handling files. Apple says it must not be terminated. It's normally light.
whyHigh: Many apps launching at once
Installing or updating apps
A problem with an app that keeps relaunching
whatToDo: Wait a minute
Look for an app that keeps crashing or relaunching
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Apple says it must not be terminated.

processes.title: iconservicesagent
processes.oneLiner: Creates the app and file icons you see in Finder, the Dock and elsewhere.
processes.summary: iconservicesagent reads icon resources from apps and the system and generates icon images at the right sizes for display. It's busiest when you see lots of new icons at once, and it caches results so the next time is quicker.
whyHigh: Browsing folders with many different apps or file types
After installing apps or a macOS update, while icons are regenerated
Connecting a drive with many apps
whatToDo: Wait; it settles once icons are cached
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches when needed; icons may appear blank for a moment.

processes.title: fontd
processes.oneLiner: Registers fonts and makes them available to every app.
processes.summary: fontd is the system font registration manager: it keeps track of installed fonts and makes them available to apps. fontworker helps with font tasks. They are busiest when fonts are installed or removed, or when an app loads a large font library.
whyHigh: Installing, removing or activating many fonts
Font manager apps or design apps loading big font collections
A damaged font file
whatToDo: Let font installs finish
Use Font Book's validation feature to find damaged fonts
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; text in open apps could briefly display oddly.

processes.title: fseventsd
processes.oneLiner: Records which folders have changed so apps like Spotlight and Time Machine can react.
processes.summary: fseventsd keeps a log of file system changes: when files are created, changed or deleted, it records which folders were affected. Spotlight, Time Machine, cloud sync apps and developer tools use this to find what changed without scanning everything. Its activity rises with how much file activity is going on.
whyHigh: Lots of files being created or changed (downloads, builds, unzipping archives)
Cloud sync or backup apps processing many changes
Developer tools watching big project folders
whatToDo: Wait for big copies, downloads or builds to finish
Pause sync apps temporarily to compare
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: Spotlight, backups and sync apps rely on it to notice changes.

processes.title: notifyd
processes.oneLiner: A tiny messaging service that lets system processes signal each other quickly.
processes.summary: notifyd is the server for the low-level notification system processes use to signal simple events to each other, such as 'the time zone changed'. It's not related to the notification banners you see. It starts at boot and is normally extremely light.
whyHigh: A process posting system events in a tight loop
Many processes starting at once
whatToDo: Look for another process that is also busy at the same time
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: many system processes depend on it.

processes.title: runningboardd
processes.oneLiner: Decides how much priority and freedom each running app and helper gets.
processes.summary: runningboardd manages process 'assertions': requests that keep an app or helper running, awake or at a certain priority while it does something important. It helps macOS decide what can be paused or limited to save energy. It's always running and normally light.
whyHigh: Many apps and helpers starting or stopping
An app repeatedly requesting and releasing assertions
whatToDo: Wait a moment after opening several apps
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: macOS uses it to manage running apps.

processes.title: dasd
processes.oneLiner: Duet Activity Scheduler: picks good moments to run background tasks like backups and indexing.
processes.summary: dasd is the Duet Activity Scheduler daemon. macOS has hundreds of background jobs (backups, Spotlight indexing, photo analysis, update checks) and dasd decides when each should run, taking into account things like battery, power, how busy you are and the time of day. It's normally light; if it seems busy, the jobs it starts are usually what's actually using resources.
whyHigh: Many background tasks being scheduled, for example after waking or plugging in
Shortly after login or a macOS update
whatToDo: Wait a few minutes
Look for the background tasks that start afterwards (backupd, mds, photoanalysisd)
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; background tasks may be delayed.

processes.title: diskarbitrationd
processes.oneLiner: Notices disks being connected and decides how and where they are mounted.
processes.summary: diskarbitrationd tells apps when disks and volumes appear or disappear and manages mounting them, for example when you plug in a USB drive or open a disk image. It's essential and normally idle.
whyHigh: Connecting drives or opening disk images
A drive or cable that keeps disconnecting and reconnecting
A damaged disk being checked
whatToDo: Eject external drives you aren't using
Try a different cable or port for a drive that keeps dropping
Run First Aid in Disk Utility on the affected disk
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: mounting and ejecting disks depend on it.

processes.title: apfsd
processes.oneLiner: Housekeeping for APFS disks: encryption, defragmentation and other maintenance.
processes.summary: apfsd is the APFS volume management daemon. APFS is the file system macOS uses, and apfsd handles volume encryption and decryption, automatic defragmentation and other housekeeping. It's busiest when FileVault is encrypting or decrypting a disk.
whyHigh: FileVault encrypting or decrypting a disk
Maintenance after connecting an external APFS drive
Lots of disk activity
whatToDo: If FileVault is encrypting, keep the Mac plugged in and let it finish
Check progress in System Settings > Privacy & Security > FileVault
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: it manages your disks and encryption.

processes.title: deleted
processes.oneLiner: Frees up 'purgeable' disk space by asking apps to clear caches when storage runs low.
processes.summary: deleted manages purgeable space: caches and other data macOS can safely remove when needed. When your disk gets low on space, deleted asks registered services to clear what they can. It's not deleting your files. It's normal for it to be busy when storage is nearly full.
whyHigh: Your disk is nearly full
A large download or app install needs space
Clearing caches after a macOS update
whatToDo: Free up space: check System Settings > General > Storage
Empty the Trash and remove large files you don't need
Wait for it to finish; restart if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; freeing space may be delayed.

processes.title: revisiond
processes.oneLiner: Stores earlier versions of your documents for 'Revert To' and 'Browse All Versions'.
processes.summary: revisiond manages document revisions: the saved versions that let you go back in apps like Pages, TextEdit and Preview using File > Revert To. It runs on demand and is normally quiet.
whyHigh: Saving large documents often
Connecting a drive with lots of document history
whatToDo: Wait for saves to finish
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches; version history could be affected if interrupted while saving.

processes.title: mobileassetd
processes.oneLiner: Downloads extra system resources from Apple, such as fonts, voices and language data.
processes.summary: mobileassetd downloads and manages optional system assets that macOS fetches on demand, such as fonts, dictionaries, voices, language data and machine-learning models used by system features. It's busiest after a macOS update or when you turn on a feature that needs new data.
whyHigh: After a macOS update, while new assets download
Turning on a feature that needs extra data (a new language, voice or dictation)
A slow or interrupted download being retried
whatToDo: Let it finish on a good network connection
Keep the Mac plugged in and awake for a while
Restart your Mac if it seems stuck
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; downloads will resume later.

processes.title: pboard
processes.oneLiner: The clipboard service: holds what you copy so you can paste it elsewhere.
processes.summary: pboard provides pasteboard (clipboard) services. When you copy something, it's kept here until you paste. It also supports drag-and-drop. It's normally idle unless very large items are being copied.
whyHigh: Copying very large images, files or amounts of text
Clipboard manager apps polling the clipboard
Universal Clipboard syncing with an iPhone or iPad
whatToDo: Copy something small to replace a huge clipboard item
Quit clipboard manager apps to compare
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches; whatever was on the clipboard is lost.

processes.title: timed
processes.oneLiner: Keeps your Mac's clock accurate by syncing with time servers.
processes.summary: timed maintains system clock accuracy by synchronizing with reference clocks over the network (using technologies such as NTP). It's aware of power and battery conditions and is normally almost idle.
whyHigh: Network changes or waking from sleep, when it rechecks the time
Time zone or date settings being changed
whatToDo: Make sure 'Set time and date automatically' is on in System Settings > General > Date & Time
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches; clock syncing pauses briefly.

processes.title: watchdogd
processes.oneLiner: Checks that macOS stays healthy and responsive, and recovers it if the system gets stuck.
processes.summary: watchdogd makes sure the system keeps making progress. If it detects that macOS is badly stuck, it takes corrective action and, as a last resort, can restart the system to get it working again. Despite the name, it's a protective part of macOS, not spyware. It's normally idle.
whyHigh: The system is under heavy strain or parts of it are unresponsive
Recovering from a hang
whatToDo: Check which apps are using lots of CPU or memory and quit them
Install the latest macOS update
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: it protects macOS from getting permanently stuck.

processes.title: sharedfilelistd
processes.oneLiner: Keeps your Recent Items, Open Recent lists and some Finder sidebar favourites.
processes.summary: sharedfilelistd is a per-user agent that manages lists of recent and favourite documents, apps and volumes. These power Apple menu > Recent Items, each app's File > Open Recent, and some Finder sidebar items. It's normally idle.
whyHigh: Very long recent-items lists
Sidebar items pointing to disconnected network drives
whatToDo: Clear recent items via Apple menu > Recent Items > Clear Menu
Remove sidebar items for drives you no longer use
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches when needed; recent items lists may briefly be empty.

processes.title: containermanagerd
processes.oneLiner: Creates and manages the private storage 'containers' that sandboxed apps keep their data in.
processes.summary: containermanagerd creates, removes and manages containers: the private folders where sandboxed apps (including most App Store apps) keep their data, separate from other apps. It works with the sandbox to keep apps isolated. It's normally light.
whyHigh: Installing, updating or first-launching sandboxed apps
After a macOS update, while containers are checked or migrated
whatToDo: Wait for installs and updates to finish
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: sandboxed apps need it to access their data.

processes.title: backgroundtaskmanagementd
processes.oneLiner: Tracks login items and background apps, and shows 'Background Items Added' notifications.
processes.summary: backgroundtaskmanagementd manages the list of items allowed to run at login or in the background, and your approval of them. BackgroundTaskManagementAgent shows the notifications you get when an app adds a background item. You can review all of these in System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions.
whyHigh: Installing or updating apps that add background items
Many login items starting after login
whatToDo: Review System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions and turn off items you don't need
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; login item notifications may be delayed.

processes.title: smd
processes.oneLiner: Installs and manages helper tools and login items that apps register with macOS.
processes.summary: smd performs operations for the ServiceManagement framework, which apps use to register login items and privileged helper tools. It's busy mainly when apps install or remove such helpers.
whyHigh: Installing or updating apps with background helpers
An app repeatedly registering its helper
whatToDo: Let installs finish
Review System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches when needed.

processes.title: analyticsd
processes.oneLiner: Collects diagnostics and usage data locally if you've opted in to share analytics with Apple.
processes.summary: analyticsd collects diagnostic and usage information locally on users' Macs that have opted in to sharing analytics. You can review or change this in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements. It's normally light.
whyHigh: Processing collected data periodically
After crashes or updates generate more diagnostic data
whatToDo: Wait; it finishes its periodic work quickly
Turn off sharing in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements if you prefer
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; nothing visible changes.

processes.title: SubmitDiagInfo
processes.oneLiner: Periodically sends diagnostic reports to Apple if you opted in, and cleans up old ones.
processes.summary: SubmitDiagInfo runs periodically. If you've opted in to share diagnostic and usage information, it sends recent reports to Apple; it also cleans up old diagnostic data. It runs briefly and exits.
whyHigh: Many crash or diagnostic reports waiting to be sent
Cleaning up a large backlog of reports
whatToDo: Let it finish; it runs briefly
Change sharing in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements
If many reports exist, check Console > Crash Reports for an app that keeps crashing
processes.safeToQuitNote: Quitting just postpones it to the next run.

processes.title: PerfPowerServices
processes.oneLiner: Keeps records of power and performance data, such as the battery usage history.
processes.summary: PerfPowerServices manages archives of power and performance data. Features like the battery usage graphs in System Settings rely on this kind of history. It's normally light and works in short bursts.
whyHigh: Periodic processing of power and performance records
After a macOS update
whatToDo: Wait; it usually settles within minutes
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; power history may have a small gap.

processes.title: systemstats
processes.oneLiner: Gathers statistics about system power use for macOS's energy tracking.
processes.summary: systemstats collects and summarises statistics about power usage, which macOS uses for things like energy and battery reporting. It runs periodically in the background and can briefly use noticeable CPU while it processes data, then settles.
whyHigh: Periodic processing of power statistics, often after waking or being idle
After a macOS update
whatToDo: Wait a few minutes; short spikes are normal
Restart your Mac if it stays busy for a long time
processes.safeToQuitNote: It runs again later; quitting just interrupts the current pass.

processes.title: usbmuxd
processes.oneLiner: Handles communication between your Mac and connected iPhones or iPads over USB or Wi-Fi.
processes.summary: usbmuxd manages communication between macOS and iOS devices, over USB cables or Wi-Fi. Finder syncing, backups, Xcode and other tools that talk to an iPhone or iPad use it. It starts at boot and is normally idle.
whyHigh: Syncing or backing up an iPhone or iPad
Xcode installing or debugging apps on a device
A flaky cable causing repeated reconnections
whatToDo: Let syncing or backup finish
Try another cable or port if the device keeps reconnecting
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; connected iPhones or iPads disconnect briefly.

processes.title: VTDecoderXPCService
processes.oneLiner: Decodes (and encodes) video for apps using Apple's VideoToolbox, often with hardware help.
processes.summary: VTDecoderXPCService decodes video for apps that use Apple's VideoToolbox framework, and VTEncoderXPCService encodes it. Browsers, video players, video-calling and screen-recording apps use them, usually with the Mac's dedicated media hardware. CPU use here simply reflects video being played, streamed or recorded by some app.
whyHigh: Watching or streaming video, especially high resolution
Video calls or screen sharing
Screen recording or video editing/exporting
Video formats your Mac can't decode in hardware
whatToDo: Pause videos and close tabs that play video, then check again
End video calls or screen recordings you don't need
Restart the app that's playing video
Restart your Mac if it stays high with no video playing
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches when needed; video in the app using it may freeze or stop.

processes.title: VDCAssistant
processes.oneLiner: Lets apps capture video from the FaceTime camera or USB webcams.
processes.summary: VDCAssistant supports video capture from some built-in FaceTime cameras and external USB webcams, and allows several apps to use the same camera at once. It's active while an app is using the camera. When the camera is in use, macOS shows the green camera light and a camera indicator in the menu bar.
whyHigh: A video call or camera app in use
An app keeping the camera open in the background
whatToDo: Check which app is using the camera (look for the camera indicator in the menu bar or Control Center)
Quit that app if you're not using it
Review camera access in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Camera
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it when needed; the camera stops working in open apps until then.

processes.title: AirPlayXPCHelper
processes.oneLiner: Helps with AirPlay: streaming audio or video, or mirroring your screen to other devices.
processes.summary: AirPlayXPCHelper is a macOS helper used by AirPlay, the feature for streaming audio and video or mirroring your screen to an Apple TV, AirPlay speaker or another Mac. It's busier while AirPlay is active and quiet otherwise.
whyHigh: AirPlay streaming or screen mirroring in progress
The Mac searching for AirPlay devices on a busy network
whatToDo: Stop AirPlay or screen mirroring if you're not using it
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches; any AirPlay stream will stop.

processes.title: PowerChime
processes.oneLiner: Plays the little chime when you plug a charger into a MacBook.
processes.summary: PowerChime is a tiny background app that plays the charging sound when you connect power to a Mac laptop. It does almost nothing the rest of the time.
whyHigh: Rarely busy; it only works for a moment when power is connected
A faulty charger or cable connecting and disconnecting repeatedly can trigger it over and over
whatToDo: Try a different charger or cable if the chime keeps playing
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches; you might miss the charging sound once.

processes.title: CoreServicesUIAgent
processes.oneLiner: Shows system dialogs, such as the warning before opening an app downloaded from the internet.
processes.summary: CoreServicesUIAgent displays certain system dialogs on behalf of macOS, including the prompts that appear when you first open an app or file downloaded from the internet. It's idle unless one of those dialogs is showing.
whyHigh: Opening a newly downloaded app while it's being checked
Several first-launch dialogs at once
whatToDo: Look for an open dialog behind other windows and respond to it
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches; any dialog it was showing closes.

processes.title: AppleSpell
processes.oneLiner: Checks spelling and grammar as you type, in every app that uses the system spell checker.
processes.summary: AppleSpell is the system spelling and grammar service. Apps send it text to check, and it returns suggestions and corrections. It's busier when you type a lot or open long documents with checking turned on.
whyHigh: Long documents with spelling or grammar checking on
Many languages enabled for automatic detection
An app sending text to check over and over
whatToDo: Wait for long documents to finish checking
Turn off grammar checking in the app's Edit > Spelling and Grammar menu
Force quit AppleSpell; it relaunches when needed
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches automatically; spell check pauses briefly.

processes.title: Open and Save Panel Service
processes.oneLiner: Shows the Open and Save dialogs for apps, keeping your files private from sandboxed apps.
processes.summary: This service draws the Open and Save dialogs in apps. For sandboxed apps, it runs outside the app so you can pick any file while the app only gets access to the one you chose. It's active while a dialog is open.
whyHigh: An Open or Save dialog browsing a huge folder or slow network drive
Cloud folders loading in the dialog
whatToDo: Close the dialog and reopen it
Avoid starting in large or network folders
Restart the app that opened the dialog
processes.safeToQuitNote: The open dialog closes; the app may need restarting to show it again.

processes.title: Virtualization.framework VM
processes.oneLiner: A virtual machine run by Apple's Virtualization framework for apps like Docker, UTM or OrbStack.
processes.summary: This process is a virtual machine created through Apple's Virtualization framework. Apps such as Docker Desktop, UTM, OrbStack and other Linux or macOS VM tools use it. Its CPU and memory reflect everything running inside that virtual machine, so it can be large; the memory you allocated to the VM is often reserved here.
whyHigh: Containers or a guest operating system doing work inside the VM
A large amount of memory assigned to the VM in the app's settings
Builds, databases or other heavy services running in containers
whatToDo: Check which app started it (Docker, UTM, OrbStack, etc.) and look at what's running inside
Stop containers or VMs you don't need
Lower the VM's memory or CPU allowance in the app's settings
Quit the app that owns the VM properly rather than force quitting this process
processes.safeToQuitNote: Force quitting it is like pulling the plug on that virtual machine; unsaved data inside it can be lost.

processes.title: securityd
processes.oneLiner: Guards your keychain and handles encryption, keeping passwords and private keys safe.
processes.summary: securityd maintains security contexts and handles cryptographic operations for macOS. Access to keychain items goes through it, so apps never get to see private keys directly and access rules are enforced. It's a core security component and normally light.
whyHigh: Apps reading many keychain items, such as a password manager or browser at launch
Certificate or code-signing checks during installs
A damaged keychain causing repeated retries
whatToDo: Wait a minute after login or after opening many apps
If you keep getting keychain password prompts, open Keychain Access and check for errors
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: keychain access, logins and encryption depend on it.

processes.title: secd
processes.oneLiner: Controls access to keychain items and keeps iCloud Keychain in sync.
processes.summary: secd is the central keychain agent: anything that needs to read or change keychain items, such as saved passwords, Wi-Fi passwords or passkeys, talks to it. It also takes part in syncing iCloud Keychain across your devices. It's normally light.
whyHigh: iCloud Keychain syncing many changes, such as after signing in on a new device
Password managers or browsers reading lots of saved passwords
A keychain problem causing repeated retries
whatToDo: Wait; sync bursts finish on their own
Make sure you're signed in to iCloud properly in System Settings
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; apps may briefly fail to read saved passwords.

processes.title: trustd
processes.oneLiner: Checks that security certificates are valid, for websites, apps and secure connections.
processes.summary: trustd evaluates trust in certificates for every process on the Mac. When an app makes a secure (HTTPS) connection or checks a signature, trustd verifies the certificate chain and may check online whether a certificate has been revoked. It's busier when lots of secure connections are being made.
whyHigh: Lots of new secure connections (browsers, sync apps, updates)
Slow or blocked access to certificate-checking servers
VPNs, proxies or security software that inspect HTTPS traffic
whatToDo: Wait; spikes during heavy browsing or updates are normal
Temporarily disable VPN or HTTPS-inspecting tools to compare
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; secure connections may fail for a moment.

processes.title: tccd
processes.oneLiner: Enforces privacy permissions: camera, microphone, screen recording, files, contacts and more.
processes.summary: tccd runs Transparency, Consent and Control (TCC), the system that asks for your permission before apps can use the camera, microphone, screen recording, your contacts, photos, certain folders or Accessibility features. It records your choices and checks them whenever an app asks. You manage these in System Settings > Privacy & Security.
whyHigh: An app repeatedly requesting a permission it doesn't have
Many apps checking permissions at once, such as after login
Monitoring or automation tools making frequent privacy-protected requests
whatToDo: Answer any pending permission prompt (it may be behind other windows)
Review System Settings > Privacy & Security and remove access for apps you don't use
Quit apps you've recently granted or denied access to, to find a repeat requester
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; apps may briefly be denied access to protected data.

processes.title: syspolicyd
processes.oneLiner: Gatekeeper's engine: checks new apps and software before macOS lets them run.
processes.summary: syspolicyd enforces macOS's system policy for what may be installed or run. It's the engine behind Gatekeeper, which checks that apps come from identified developers and have been notarized by Apple, and it may check online with Apple when you first open something. It's busiest when new or changed software runs for the first time.
whyHigh: Opening newly downloaded or updated apps
Installing large apps or many command-line tools at once
Software builds that create many new programs
A slow connection while it checks with Apple
whatToDo: Wait; first-launch checks finish on their own
Let installers and updates complete before opening the new apps
Restart your Mac if it stays high
Keep Gatekeeper on; it protects you from malware
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; new apps may fail to open until it's back.

processes.title: XProtect (XprotectService)
processes.oneLiner: macOS's built-in anti-malware: scans apps for known malware and removes infections.
processes.summary: XProtect is the antivirus technology built into macOS. It checks apps for known malware when they're first opened or changed, and its companion XProtect Remediator scans in the background periodically and removes known threats. Apple updates its malware definitions automatically. Seeing these processes is a good sign: it means your Mac's built-in protection is working.
whyHigh: Opening newly downloaded or updated apps, which get scanned
A periodic background malware scan
Just after XProtect's definitions were updated
Large apps or archives with many files to check
whatToDo: Let the scan finish; it usually takes seconds to a few minutes
Keep 'Install Security Responses and system files' on in System Settings > General > Software Update > Automatic Updates
Restart your Mac if it stays busy for a long time
Don't try to disable it; it protects you from malware
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches these when needed; quitting just interrupts a scan.

processes.title: endpointsecurityd
processes.oneLiner: Runs and supervises security tools (antivirus, monitoring) that use Apple's Endpoint Security system.
processes.summary: endpointsecurityd manages the user-space parts of Apple's Endpoint Security system, which antivirus, firewall and company security tools use to watch for threats. It starts those tools' system extensions and monitors their health. If you don't have such software, it does very little.
whyHigh: Antivirus or company security software actively scanning
A security tool that is struggling or unresponsive
Lots of file and process activity being monitored
whatToDo: Check which security or monitoring tools are installed (System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions)
Update or restart that security software
On a work Mac, contact your IT team before removing anything
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: security tools that protect your Mac depend on it.

processes.title: amfid
processes.oneLiner: Checks code signatures to make sure programs haven't been tampered with before they run.
processes.summary: amfid (Apple Mobile File Integrity daemon) checks the integrity of programs running on the system, helping ensure that code is properly signed and hasn't been modified. It works mostly when new or unusual programs start.
whyHigh: Many new programs launching, such as during software builds or installs
Command-line tools being run in large numbers
whatToDo: Wait for builds and installs to finish
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: Don't quit it: programs may fail to launch without it.

processes.title: sandboxd
processes.oneLiner: Supports the app sandbox, which limits what apps can access, and logs blocked attempts.
processes.summary: sandboxd performs services for the macOS sandbox, the security boundary that limits what apps and system services can touch. It notably reports when something tries to do what its sandbox doesn't allow. Busy periods usually mean some app keeps bumping into its limits.
whyHigh: An app repeatedly trying to access something it isn't allowed to
Lots of sandbox violations being logged after an update
whatToDo: Look in the Console app for 'Sandbox' messages to see which app is involved
Update or restart that app
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; there's no benefit in quitting it.

processes.title: coreauthd
processes.oneLiner: Handles Touch ID and password prompts when apps ask you to confirm it's you.
processes.summary: coreauthd provides Local Authentication services: when an app or the system asks you to confirm your identity with Touch ID, your Apple Watch or your password, coreauthd manages that check and shows the prompt. It's idle the rest of the time.
whyHigh: Authentication prompts appearing repeatedly
Password managers or apps requesting Touch ID often
whatToDo: Respond to any pending authentication prompt
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; a prompt on screen will be cancelled.

processes.title: socketfilterfw
processes.oneLiner: The built-in macOS firewall, controlling which apps may accept incoming connections.
processes.summary: socketfilterfw is part of macOS's Application Firewall. It's started on demand when the firewall is turned on, and it decides whether apps may accept incoming network connections. You control it in System Settings > Network > Firewall.
whyHigh: Many incoming connection attempts on a busy network
Apps that open network services, such as developer servers or file sharing
whatToDo: Check firewall options in System Settings > Network > Firewall
Quit apps that run local servers if you don't need them
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it when needed; keep the firewall on for protection.

processes.title: nehelper
processes.oneLiner: Manages settings for VPNs, content filters and other Network Extension apps.
processes.summary: nehelper is part of Apple's Network Extension framework, used by VPN apps, content filters, firewalls and DNS tools. It hands out and applies their network configurations. If you don't use such apps it does very little.
whyHigh: A VPN or filter app repeatedly changing its configuration
Connecting and disconnecting VPNs
Several network-filtering apps installed at once
whatToDo: Check VPN and filter apps in System Settings > Network and > VPN
Disconnect or quit VPN and filter apps to compare
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; VPNs and filters may briefly disconnect.

processes.title: cloudd
processes.oneLiner: Syncs app data with iCloud using CloudKit, for Apple apps and many third-party apps.
processes.summary: cloudd is the daemon behind CloudKit, the service many apps use to sync data through iCloud, including Notes, Reminders, Safari, Messages in iCloud and lots of third-party apps. Its activity rises when there's lots to sync, such as after signing in to iCloud on a new Mac.
whyHigh: First iCloud sync after setting up a Mac or signing in
Large amounts of data changing in apps that sync with iCloud
A slow or unreliable internet connection causing retries
An app stuck repeatedly trying to sync
whatToDo: Leave the Mac on and connected for a while so sync can finish
Check iCloud status in System Settings > [your name] > iCloud
Quit apps that are syncing heavily, then reopen them
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; syncing simply pauses and resumes.

processes.title: bird
processes.oneLiner: Syncs iCloud Drive (including Desktop and Documents if enabled) with iCloud.
processes.summary: bird is one of the daemons behind iCloud Drive. It keeps your iCloud Drive files, and your Desktop and Documents folders if you turned that on, in sync with iCloud. It's busy when lots of files are being uploaded or downloaded, which can take a while after setup or big changes.
whyHigh: Uploading or downloading many or large files to iCloud Drive
First sync after enabling iCloud Drive or Desktop & Documents
Optimised storage removing or re-downloading files
Sync errors causing retries
whatToDo: Check progress in Finder's iCloud Drive sidebar (look for the progress circle)
Leave the Mac on, plugged in and connected so it can finish
Avoid keeping huge, constantly changing files (like VMs or databases) in iCloud Drive
Restart your Mac if it seems stuck
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; iCloud Drive syncing pauses and resumes.

typical.cpu: Near 0% when idle; higher while syncing

processes.title: fileproviderd
processes.oneLiner: Connects Finder with cloud storage like iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive and Google Drive.
processes.summary: fileproviderd coordinates File Provider extensions, the modern way cloud storage apps plug into Finder. iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive and others use it to show cloud files, download them on demand and keep them in sync. High activity usually means one of those services is syncing many files.
whyHigh: A cloud storage app syncing or indexing lots of files
Several cloud services installed at once
Spotlight indexing a large cloud folder
A sync conflict or error looping
whatToDo: Check each cloud app (iCloud, Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive) for sync status
Pause syncing in one app at a time to find the busy one
Update the cloud storage apps
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; cloud folders may briefly disappear from Finder.

processes.title: cloudphotod
processes.oneLiner: Uploads and downloads your photos and videos for iCloud Photos.
processes.summary: cloudphotod is the iCloud Photos agent. It's responsible for syncing your photo library with iCloud: uploading new photos and videos and downloading ones from your other devices. The first sync of a big library can take many hours or days.
whyHigh: Syncing a large library, especially the first time
Importing many photos or videos
Downloading originals because 'Download Originals' is on
whatToDo: Check progress at the bottom of the Library view in the Photos app
Keep the Mac plugged in and connected, and let it run overnight
Pause syncing temporarily from the Photos app if you need the bandwidth
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; syncing just pauses and resumes.

processes.title: photolibraryd
processes.oneLiner: Handles all requests to your Photos library, from the Photos app and other apps.
processes.summary: photolibraryd is the photo library agent: it handles requests to read and update your Photos library, whether from the Photos app, the photo picker in other apps, or iCloud Photos. It's busiest when importing, syncing or editing lots of photos.
whyHigh: Importing or syncing many photos
Upgrading the library after a macOS update
Apps browsing the photo library
whatToDo: Let imports and syncs finish
Keep the Mac plugged in after a macOS update so library upgrades complete
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; the Photos app may need to be reopened.

processes.title: photoanalysisd
processes.oneLiner: Analyses your photos in the background for Memories, People and searching by what's in them.
processes.summary: photoanalysisd processes your photo library in the background to power Memories, People & Pets and searching for things like 'beach' or 'dog'. The analysis happens on your Mac. It often runs when your Mac is idle and plugged in, and it can take a long time for a big library, after which it calms down.
whyHigh: A new or large photo library being analysed
After a macOS update, when analysis may be redone
Importing many new photos
whatToDo: Leave the Mac plugged in and idle (for example overnight) so it can finish
Quit the Photos app; analysis often runs while it's closed and the Mac is idle
Restart your Mac if it seems stuck for days
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it later; quitting only delays the analysis.

processes.title: mediaanalysisd
processes.oneLiner: Analyses images and video for features like Live Text, Visual Look Up and photo search.
processes.summary: mediaanalysisd analyses images and video to power features such as Live Text (selecting text in pictures), Visual Look Up (identifying plants, landmarks and more) and searching your photos. Much of the work runs on your Mac using the Neural Engine; Visual Look Up can also contact Apple's servers to fetch results. It's busiest after updates or when lots of new media arrives.
whyHigh: Analysing a large photo library or many new photos and videos
After a macOS or Photos update
Syncing with iCloud Photos
Using Visual Look Up or Live Text on images
whatToDo: Leave the Mac plugged in and idle (for example overnight) so analysis can finish
Quit the Photos app while you work
Restart your Mac if it stays very high for days
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it later; quitting just postpones the work.

processes.title: nsurlsessiond
processes.oneLiner: Does background downloads and uploads for apps, even after you close them.
processes.summary: nsurlsessiond performs background network transfers for apps that use Apple's background download system. App Store downloads, iCloud, Music, Podcasts, updates and many third-party apps hand their transfers to it so they can continue even if the app quits. High network activity here means some app is downloading or uploading.
whyHigh: App, system or podcast downloads in progress
iCloud or other sync services transferring data
Apps downloading large content in the background
whatToDo: Check App Store, Music, Podcasts and iCloud for active downloads
Let large transfers finish on a good connection
Restart your Mac if it seems stuck
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; downloads pause and usually resume later.

processes.title: apsd
processes.oneLiner: Keeps a connection to Apple's push notification service so apps get messages instantly.
processes.summary: apsd is the Apple Push Notification service daemon. It keeps one efficient connection open to Apple's servers so that messages, notifications and iCloud changes can be pushed to your Mac right away, instead of every app checking constantly. Having it connected to Apple's servers is normal.
whyHigh: Lots of incoming pushes (messages, iCloud changes)
An unreliable network causing reconnects
Firewalls or VPNs blocking Apple's push servers
whatToDo: Check your network connection
Temporarily disconnect VPNs or filters to compare
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; notifications and messages may arrive late until it reconnects.

processes.title: akd
processes.oneLiner: Handles Apple Account sign-in and authentication for iCloud, the App Store and other services.
processes.summary: akd is the AuthKit daemon, which manages Apple Account authentication on your Mac: signing in, verifying your account, two-factor codes, and keeping sign-in tokens fresh for services like iCloud and the App Store. It's normally idle.
whyHigh: Signing in to an Apple Account or verifying it
An account problem causing repeated authentication attempts
Changing your Apple Account password
whatToDo: Check System Settings > [your name] for sign-in prompts or warnings
Sign out and back in to your Apple Account if prompts keep appearing
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; sign-ins may briefly fail.

processes.title: accountsd
processes.oneLiner: Stores your internet accounts (iCloud, Google, Microsoft and others) and shares them with apps.
processes.summary: accountsd manages the accounts you add in System Settings > Internet Accounts, such as iCloud, Google, Microsoft Exchange and others. Apps like Mail, Calendar and Contacts ask it for account details instead of storing your credentials themselves. It's normally light.
whyHigh: Mail, Calendar or Contacts syncing many accounts
An account with a wrong password causing repeated retries
Adding or removing accounts
whatToDo: Check System Settings > Internet Accounts for accounts showing errors
Re-enter passwords or remove accounts you no longer use
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; apps may briefly lose access to accounts.

processes.title: imagent
processes.oneLiner: The background agent for Messages and FaceTime, sending and receiving your iMessages.
processes.summary: imagent runs in the background for Messages (and related FaceTime functions), keeping your iMessage and SMS conversations in sync even when the Messages app is closed. It's busier when lots of messages arrive or when Messages in iCloud is syncing.
whyHigh: Many messages or attachments arriving
Messages in iCloud syncing a large history
Group chats with lots of activity
whatToDo: Let sync finish; check Messages > Settings > iMessage
Restart the Messages app
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; messages may be delayed briefly.

processes.title: identityservicesd
processes.oneLiner: Registers your devices with Apple so iMessage, FaceTime and Continuity can reach them.
processes.summary: identityservicesd runs Apple's Identity Services, which register your Mac and your other Apple devices under your Apple Account. iMessage, FaceTime, Handoff and other Continuity features use it to find and securely message your devices. It's normally light.
whyHigh: Signing in to iMessage or FaceTime
Many devices on your Apple Account syncing
