Network problems causing retries
whatToDo: Wait a few minutes after signing in
Check your network connection
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; messages and calls may be briefly delayed.

processes.title: callservicesd
processes.oneLiner: Keeps track of phone and FaceTime calls on your Mac, including calls from your iPhone.
processes.summary: callservicesd is the system daemon that maintains call state: it tracks FaceTime calls and iPhone calls you make or receive on your Mac through Continuity, and keeps call history in sync. It's usually idle unless a call is happening.
whyHigh: An active call
Syncing call history
Your iPhone nearby with many incoming calls
whatToDo: End any active calls
If you don't take calls on your Mac, turn off 'Calls from iPhone' in FaceTime settings
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; any active call may drop.

processes.title: avconferenced
processes.oneLiner: Handles the audio and video of FaceTime calls.
processes.summary: avconferenced handles real-time audio and video conferencing for Apple's calling features such as FaceTime. It's active during calls, when it encodes and decodes audio and video, and idle otherwise.
whyHigh: An active FaceTime call, especially a video or group call
Screen sharing during a call
whatToDo: End calls you're not using
Restart your Mac if it stays busy after calls end
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches when needed; any active call will drop.

processes.title: CommCenter
processes.oneLiner: Lets your Mac make and receive phone calls through your iPhone.
processes.summary: CommCenter provides the functionality that allows phone calls to be made and received on your Mac, using your nearby iPhone's cellular connection. It runs in the background and is normally light.
whyHigh: Calls or text messages relayed from your iPhone
Your iPhone repeatedly connecting and disconnecting
whatToDo: If you don't use iPhone calls on your Mac, turn off 'Calls from iPhone' in FaceTime settings
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; calls from iPhone may briefly not ring on your Mac.

processes.title: sharingd
processes.oneLiner: Powers AirDrop, Handoff, Instant Hotspot and other sharing features.
processes.summary: sharingd enables AirDrop file sharing, Handoff between your devices, Instant Hotspot, connecting to shared computers and Remote Disc. It keeps an eye out for nearby Apple devices, so some background activity is normal.
whyHigh: AirDrop transfers or AirDrop open to Everyone in a crowded place
Handoff and Universal Clipboard activity
Many Apple devices nearby
whatToDo: Set AirDrop to Contacts Only or off in Control Center when not using it
Turn off Handoff in System Settings > General > AirDrop & Handoff if you don't use it
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; an AirDrop transfer in progress will fail.

processes.title: rapportd
processes.oneLiner: Lets your Apple devices talk to each other for Continuity features like call handoff.
processes.summary: rapportd enables communication between your Apple devices for Continuity features such as phone call handoff, and other features that need nearby devices to coordinate. It's normal for it to make local network connections, and it's typically light.
whyHigh: Several Apple devices nearby or on the same network
Continuity features in use
Network or Bluetooth issues causing reconnects
whatToDo: Wait; activity usually settles
Turn Wi-Fi and Bluetooth off and on
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; Continuity features may pause briefly.

processes.title: searchpartyd
processes.oneLiner: Part of Find My: handles the encrypted offline finding network for your devices and AirTags.
processes.summary: searchpartyd is part of Apple's Find My system. It's associated with offline finding, the encrypted network that lets your Apple devices and AirTags be located even when they're not online, and does cryptographic work for it. It's normally light, though users have reported occasional busy periods.
whyHigh: Many devices or AirTags associated with your Apple Account
Find My syncing after changes
Bluetooth problems
whatToDo: Wait; busy periods usually pass
Open the Find My app once and allow any requested permissions
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; Find My features may pause briefly.

processes.title: findmydeviced
processes.oneLiner: The daemon for Find My Mac, so you can locate, lock or erase your Mac if it's lost.
processes.summary: findmydeviced runs Find My Mac. It lets you locate your Mac on a map, play a sound, lock it or erase it remotely if it's lost or stolen. It's normally idle.
whyHigh: Find My settings being changed
Location being requested for your Mac
whatToDo: Check Find My settings in System Settings > [your name] > iCloud
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; keep Find My on to protect a lost Mac.

processes.title: contactsd
processes.oneLiner: Manages your contacts database for the Contacts app and any app allowed to use contacts.
processes.summary: contactsd manages the information in your contacts database. It serves the Contacts app and other apps using the Contacts API, and performs background maintenance. Apps need your permission to read your contacts.
whyHigh: Syncing a large address book from iCloud, Google or Exchange
Background maintenance after a macOS update
An app reading contacts repeatedly
whatToDo: Let sync finish
Check which apps have contacts access in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Contacts
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; contacts may briefly not load in apps.

processes.title: homed
processes.oneLiner: Manages your HomeKit home and controls smart home accessories.
processes.summary: homed manages your home state and controls HomeKit accessories such as lights, plugs and cameras, for the Home app and features that use it. If you don't use HomeKit it does very little.
whyHigh: Many HomeKit accessories, or cameras streaming
Accessories that are unreachable, causing retries
Home data syncing via iCloud
whatToDo: Check the Home app for accessories marked 'No Response'
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; Home controls may be unavailable briefly.

processes.title: chronod
processes.oneLiner: Manages widgets, deciding when they refresh their content.
processes.summary: chronod is part of the system that runs widgets on your desktop and in Notification Center. It manages widget timelines, meaning when each widget should update its content. Lots of widgets that refresh often can make it busier.
whyHigh: Many widgets, especially ones that update often
A widget that keeps failing and retrying
Adding or removing widgets
whatToDo: Remove widgets you don't use
Update apps that provide widgets
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; widgets may briefly show placeholders.

processes.title: AMPDeviceDiscoveryAgent
processes.oneLiner: Detects connected iPhones, iPads and iPods so Finder can sync and back them up.
processes.summary: AMPDeviceDiscoveryAgent is a per-user agent that discovers attached iPhones, iPads and iPods, so they appear in the Finder sidebar for syncing, backups and updates. It's normally idle.
whyHigh: Connecting a device, or a cable that keeps disconnecting
Devices on the same Wi-Fi set to sync over Wi-Fi
whatToDo: Try another cable or port
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; connected devices may briefly disappear from Finder.

processes.title: Keychain Circle Notification
processes.oneLiner: Shows iCloud Keychain prompts, such as approving a new device or entering a device passcode.
processes.summary: Keychain Circle Notification shows notifications and prompts related to iCloud Keychain, for example asking you to approve a new device or enter the password of another device to keep your passwords syncing. It's idle unless such a prompt is needed.
whyHigh: A pending iCloud Keychain approval or sign-in prompt
Changes to devices on your Apple Account
whatToDo: Respond to any iCloud prompt in System Settings > [your name]
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches; an open prompt will reappear later.

processes.title: mds
processes.oneLiner: The Spotlight metadata server: coordinates indexing so you can search your Mac instantly.
processes.summary: mds is the metadata server behind Spotlight. It coordinates indexing of your files, hands work to mdworker processes that read the files, and answers searches from Spotlight, Finder and other apps. Heavy activity is normal after a macOS update, after restoring or migrating files, or when you connect a new drive, and it settles once indexing is done.
whyHigh: Indexing after a macOS update, migration or restore
A new external drive connected, or large numbers of files added or changed
Cloud folders or developer folders with many files changing constantly
A damaged index being rebuilt
whatToDo: Let it finish: keep the Mac on and plugged in; indexing can take hours on large disks
Exclude folders you never search (build folders, VM images, backups) in System Settings > Spotlight > Search Privacy
If it runs for days, rebuild the index: add your disk to Search Privacy, then remove it again
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it right away; search may be incomplete while indexing continues.

processes.title: mds_stores
processes.oneLiner: Maintains Spotlight's search index on disk, updating it as files change.
processes.summary: mds_stores manages the Spotlight index database itself, writing new and changed information that mdworker processes extract from your files. It's often the process people notice using lots of CPU or disk while Spotlight indexes, and it calms down once the index is up to date.
whyHigh: Spotlight indexing after a macOS update, migration or new drive
Many files being added or changed (downloads, syncing, builds)
A large or damaged index being rebuilt
whatToDo: Let indexing finish with the Mac plugged in; check progress by searching in Spotlight
Exclude busy folders you never search in System Settings > Spotlight > Search Privacy
If it never settles, rebuild the index by adding your disk to Search Privacy and then removing it
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; indexing resumes where it left off.

typical.cpu: Near 0% when idle; high while indexing

processes.title: mdworker
processes.oneLiner: A Spotlight worker that reads files and extracts searchable details for the index.
processes.summary: mdworker is the metadata server worker: mds starts mdworker processes to scan and index files when a drive is mounted or files change. Each one reads files of certain types and extracts text and details for Spotlight. Several can run at once and they quit when the work is done.
whyHigh: Lots of new or changed files to index
Large documents, PDFs or mail archives
A file that a Spotlight importer struggles with
whatToDo: Let indexing finish
Exclude folders you don't need searchable in System Settings > Spotlight > Search Privacy
Restart your Mac if the same worker stays busy for hours
processes.safeToQuitNote: mds simply starts a new worker; quitting doesn't stop indexing.

processes.title: mdworker_shared
processes.oneLiner: Spotlight indexing worker; modern macOS runs several at once to read files for search.
processes.summary: mdworker_shared is the form of the Spotlight worker that current macOS mostly uses. Spotlight starts these workers to read different kinds of files and extract text and details for search. You'll often see several at a time, and they come and go as needed.
whyHigh: Indexing after a macOS update, migration or new drive
Many new or changed files, like downloads, photos or code
Large or complex documents
whatToDo: Let indexing finish with the Mac on and plugged in
Exclude folders you never search in System Settings > Spotlight > Search Privacy
Restart your Mac if they stay busy for days
processes.safeToQuitNote: Spotlight starts new workers as needed; quitting one doesn't stop indexing.

typical.cpu: 0% when idle; can be 10–100% each while indexing

processes.title: corespotlightd
processes.oneLiner: Indexes content that apps share with Spotlight, like emails, notes and messages.
processes.summary: corespotlightd handles Core Spotlight, which lets apps add their own content to Spotlight search, such as emails in Mail, notes, messages and items from third-party apps. It's busier when apps donate lots of content, for example after setting up a mail account.
whyHigh: Mail, Notes, Messages or other apps indexing lots of content
Setting up accounts with large histories
Rebuilding the Spotlight index
whatToDo: Let indexing finish
In System Settings > Spotlight, turn off categories you never search
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; some search results may be missing briefly.

processes.title: Spotlight
processes.oneLiner: The Spotlight search window and menu bar search you open with Command-Space.
processes.summary: The Spotlight process runs the search interface you open with Command-Space or the magnifying glass in the menu bar. The indexing behind it is done by other processes (mds, mds_stores and mdworker). It's normally idle unless you're searching.
whyHigh: Typing searches while results load
Online suggestions loading on a slow connection
A glitch after waking from sleep
whatToDo: Close the Spotlight window
Force quit Spotlight; it relaunches automatically
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches automatically; nothing is lost.

processes.title: backupd (Time Machine)
processes.oneLiner: Runs Time Machine backups and manages your backup history.
processes.summary: backupd is the Time Machine backup daemon. It creates your backups, usually every hour when the backup disk is available, and manages old backups. It can use noticeable CPU and disk while backing up, especially the first backup, which copies everything and can take many hours.
whyHigh: The first backup to a new disk
Lots of changed files since the last backup
Backing up over a network to a slow drive
Verifying or cleaning up old backups
whatToDo: Let the backup finish; check progress in System Settings > General > Time Machine
Exclude large folders you don't need backed up (VMs, caches, downloads) in Time Machine Options
Keep the Mac plugged in and connected to the backup disk
Restart your Mac if a backup seems stuck
processes.safeToQuitNote: Quitting interrupts the current backup; skip a backup properly from the Time Machine menu instead.

processes.title: softwareupdated
processes.oneLiner: Checks for, downloads and prepares macOS updates.
processes.summary: softwareupdated is the main daemon for macOS software updates. It checks Apple's servers for updates, downloads them, and prepares them for installation. Preparing a big macOS update can use a lot of CPU and disk for a while, which is normal.
whyHigh: Downloading or preparing a macOS update
Background update checks
A stuck or failed update being retried
whatToDo: Let the update finish downloading and preparing, with the Mac plugged in
Check System Settings > General > Software Update for status
Restart your Mac if it seems stuck for hours
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; an update in progress may need to restart its preparation.

processes.title: storedownloadd
processes.oneLiner: Downloads apps and updates from the Mac App Store.
processes.summary: storedownloadd handles downloads from the Mac App Store, including new apps and app updates. It's busy while downloads are in progress and idle otherwise.
whyHigh: App Store downloads or automatic app updates
Large apps such as Xcode
A stuck download being retried
whatToDo: Check the App Store app for downloads in progress
Let large downloads finish
Restart your Mac if a download is stuck
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; downloads pause and resume.

processes.title: appstoreagent
processes.oneLiner: Background support for the Mac App Store: purchases, update checks and installs.
processes.summary: appstoreagent provides background support for the App Store, such as checking for app updates and coordinating purchases and installs. It's normally idle.
whyHigh: Checking for or installing app updates
Many apps updating at once
whatToDo: Let updates finish in the App Store app
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
processes.safeToQuitNote: It relaunches when needed.

processes.title: installd
processes.oneLiner: Installs software packages, including App Store apps and macOS components.
processes.summary: installd is used by the system during package installation, for App Store apps, system components and .pkg installers. It's busy only while something is installing.
whyHigh: Apps or updates being installed
Large installers such as Xcode or creative suites
whatToDo: Let the installation finish
Restart your Mac if an install seems stuck
processes.safeToQuitNote: Quitting can break an installation in progress; let it finish.

processes.title: assistantd (Siri)
processes.oneLiner: Siri's background service, which handles your requests to Siri.
processes.summary: assistantd is the daemon that enables Siri features, and Siri is the process for Siri's on-screen interface. They're active when you use Siri and may do some background work. If Siri is turned off in System Settings, they're usually quiet.
whyHigh: Using Siri or dictation
Background syncing of Siri data
After a macOS update
whatToDo: Wait a few minutes
If you don't use Siri, turn it off in System Settings > Siri (or Apple Intelligence & Siri)
Restart your Mac

Refreshing suggestion data in the background

Restart your Mac

After a macOS update
Rebuilding its data after the Trial folder changed

Lots of app activity

Restart your Mac if it stays busy

whyHigh: Processing location history
After a macOS update
whatToDo: Wait; it's usually brief

whyHigh: Apps or widgets (like Weather or Find My) requesting location often
Moving between places or networks
Time zone being set automatically

Turn off location for apps that don't need it
Restart your Mac

Restart your Mac

A single website misbehaving

A page stuck running scripts in a loop
Many tabs open, each needing memory
Extensions injecting code into pages

Many tabs refreshing or loading at once
Websites polling constantly in the background

Quit and reopen Safari or the app using it

Animated or 3D websites and web games
Video calls in the browser

Quit and reopen Safari
Restart your Mac if it stays high with no media playing

Building, especially clean builds of large projects
SwiftUI previews rendering
Running apps in the Simulator or debugging

Switching branches, so lots of code changed at once

Delete Derived Data (Xcode Settings > Locations) and restart Xcode if it stays stuck

Complex code that is slow to type-check
Building large dependencies or packages

Homebrew or package managers compiling from source
Linking large projects

Check Terminal or Xcode for a build you didn't mean to start
Stop the build if needed (Control-C in Terminal, or Stop in Xcode)

Live-rendering custom views in the canvas

Xcode querying devices at launch

Builds or databases running in containers

Many files open in tabs
Plugins running
whatToDo: Close files and tabs you aren't using
Split very large files into smaller ones
Quit and reopen Figma, and keep it updated
processes.safeToQuitNote: Safe to quit; Figma saves to the cloud automatically.
keywords: Figma using a lot of memory

processes.title: Obsidian
processes.oneLiner: The Obsidian notes app (built on Electron) and its helper processes.
processes.summary: Obsidian is a Markdown notes app built with Electron, so it runs a main process plus Renderer, GPU and utility helpers. Large vaults, the graph view and community plugins are the usual reasons for higher usage.
whyHigh: Indexing a large vault after opening it
Graph view open with many notes
Community plugins doing background work
Sync running
whatToDo: Close the graph view when not needed
Disable community plugins one at a time to find a heavy one
Quit and reopen Obsidian
processes.safeToQuitNote: Safe to quit; notes are saved as files as you type.

processes.title: Claude (desktop app)
processes.oneLiner: Anthropic's Claude desktop app (built on Electron) and its helper processes.
processes.summary: The Claude desktop app is built with Electron, so it runs a main process plus Renderer, GPU and utility helpers like a web browser. Long conversations and connected tools can increase its memory use. The AI itself runs on Anthropic's servers, not on your Mac.
whyHigh: Very long conversations with lots of content
Connected tools or extensions running
Long uptime without restarting the app
whatToDo: Start a new conversation for new topics
Quit and reopen the app
Keep the app updated
processes.safeToQuitNote: Safe to quit; your conversations are saved to your account.

processes.title: Parallels Desktop
processes.oneLiner: Parallels Desktop, which runs Windows or other operating systems in virtual machines.
processes.summary: Parallels Desktop runs virtual machines on your Mac. prl_vm_app is a running virtual machine, prl_disp_service is the background service that manages VMs, and prl_client_app is the Parallels interface. A running VM's CPU and memory reflect everything happening inside Windows or the other guest system.
whyHigh: A virtual machine running, especially Windows updates or antivirus scans inside it
Large memory assigned to the VM
Games or heavy apps inside the VM
whatToDo: Check what's running inside the VM (for example Windows Task Manager)
Suspend or shut down VMs you aren't using
Lower the VM's CPU and memory in its configuration
Keep Parallels Desktop and its Tools updated
processes.safeToQuitNote: Force quitting prl_vm_app is like pulling the plug on that VM; shut it down or suspend it from Parallels instead.

processes.title: oahd (Rosetta 2)
processes.oneLiner: Rosetta 2: translates Intel-only apps so they can run on Apple silicon Macs.
processes.summary: oahd is part of Rosetta 2, the technology that lets apps built for Intel Macs run on Apple silicon. The first time you open an Intel app, or after it updates, Rosetta translates it and saves the result, which can briefly use a lot of CPU. Later launches reuse the translation and are much lighter.
whyHigh: Opening an Intel-only app for the first time
An Intel app was just updated and needs translating again
Installers or command-line tools built for Intel
whatToDo: Wait; translation is a one-time cost per app version
Check if the app has an Apple silicon version (Get Info on the app shows its Kind as 'Universal' or 'Apple Silicon')
Update or replace Intel-only apps where possible
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; the Intel app being translated may fail to open until it does.

processes.title: caffeinate
processes.oneLiner: A built-in tool that keeps your Mac awake while something is running.
processes.summary: caffeinate is a command-line tool included with macOS that stops the Mac from going to sleep, either for a set time or while another program runs. Apps, scripts and developer tools use it to keep the Mac awake during long tasks. It uses almost no CPU; its only effect is preventing sleep.
whyHigh: It almost never uses CPU; its effect is on sleep, not performance
A script or app started it and forgot to stop it, keeping the Mac awake
whatToDo: Check which app or Terminal window started it
Run 'pmset -g assertions' in Terminal to see what's keeping the Mac awake
Quit it if you want the Mac to be able to sleep again
processes.safeToQuitNote: Safe to quit; your Mac will simply be allowed to sleep normally again.

processes.title: zsh (shell)
processes.oneLiner: The command-line shell that runs inside Terminal windows and scripts.
processes.summary: zsh is the Z shell, macOS's default command-line interpreter. Every Terminal window or tab runs one, and apps and scripts also start shells to run commands. A name starting with a dash (like -zsh) is a login shell. An idle shell uses virtually no resources; high usage comes from what's running in it.
whyHigh: A script or command running in the shell
Shell startup files (like .zshrc) doing slow work
Prompt plug-ins checking git status in large folders
whatToDo: Check the Terminal window it belongs to and stop the running command with Control-C
Close Terminal windows you don't need
Simplify slow shell startup scripts or prompt themes
processes.safeToQuitNote: Quitting closes that terminal session and stops whatever was running in it.

processes.title: mdmclient
processes.oneLiner: Apple's device-management client; it's on every Mac but only acts if the Mac is enrolled.
processes.summary: mdmclient is Apple's built-in client for Mobile Device Management (MDM), which organisations use to manage work and school Macs. ManagedClient applies managed preferences and configuration profiles. These are part of every copy of macOS, so seeing them doesn't mean your Mac is being managed. To check, look at System Settings > General > Device Management (or Profiles).
whyHigh: Your organisation's management server sending profiles, apps or commands
Checking in with a management server
Applying configuration profiles after an update
whatToDo: Check System Settings > General > Device Management to see if any profiles are installed
On a work or school Mac, contact your IT team about persistent activity
If you see a profile you don't recognise on a personal Mac, review it and remove it there
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; on a managed Mac, management tasks are just delayed.

processes.title: neagent
processes.oneLiner: Hosts Network Extension plug-ins, such as VPN and content filter components from apps.
processes.summary: neagent is part of Apple's Network Extension framework. It hosts Network Extension plug-ins, including the provider extensions that VPN, proxy and content-filtering apps use. Its activity reflects the network traffic those plug-ins handle.
whyHigh: A VPN or filter app handling lots of traffic
VPN connecting and disconnecting repeatedly
whatToDo: Check VPN and filter apps in System Settings > Network and > VPN
Disconnect or quit VPN and filter apps to compare
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: VPNs or filters it hosts may disconnect until it restarts.

processes.title: networkserviceproxy
processes.oneLiner: A transparent network proxy for Apple system services, used by features like iCloud Private Relay.
processes.summary: networkserviceproxy runs the control side of Apple's NetworkServiceProxy framework, a transparent proxy used by Apple system services, including features such as iCloud Private Relay. It's normally light; more traffic through those features means more activity.
whyHigh: Heavy browsing with iCloud Private Relay turned on
Network changes causing it to reconfigure
whatToDo: Wait; activity follows your network use
Check Private Relay in System Settings > [your name] > iCloud
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; some connections may briefly fail.

processes.title: replayd
processes.oneLiner: Handles screen and in-app recording and broadcasting for apps that use ReplayKit.
processes.summary: replayd implements ReplayKit's in-app capture, recording and broadcast features on macOS. It's active while an app is recording or broadcasting and idle otherwise. If you're not recording, an app that started a recording session may still be holding it open.
whyHigh: Screen or in-app recording in progress
Live broadcasting from an app or game
whatToDo: Stop any recording or broadcast
Check which apps have screen recording access in System Settings > Privacy & Security
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Any recording in progress stops.

processes.title: biometrickitd
processes.oneLiner: Supports Touch ID fingerprint operations.
processes.summary: biometrickitd provides support for biometric operations, which on a Mac means Touch ID. It's involved when you use your fingerprint to unlock, approve purchases or fill passwords. Your fingerprint data is protected by the Secure Enclave and isn't something apps can read.
whyHigh: Using Touch ID repeatedly
Enrolling a new fingerprint
whatToDo: Wait; it's usually brief
Restart your Mac if Touch ID stops responding
processes.safeToQuitNote: Touch ID may stop working until macOS restarts it.

processes.title: System Settings
processes.oneLiner: The app where you change your Mac's settings.
processes.summary: System Settings (called System Preferences before macOS Ventura) is where you configure your Mac. It loads settings panels on demand, and some panels, such as Storage, can do heavy work while open. It's safe to quit anytime.
whyHigh: The Storage panel calculating disk usage
Searching settings for the first time
A stuck settings panel
whatToDo: Close System Settings when you're done
Force quit and reopen it if a panel is stuck
processes.safeToQuitNote: Safe to quit; changes you've made are already saved.

processes.title: talagentd
processes.oneLiner: Helps apps restore their windows and state when you reopen them (Transparent App Lifecycle).
processes.summary: talagentd provides services for macOS's Transparent App Lifecycle features, which help apps save and restore their state, such as reopening windows when you relaunch an app or log back in. It's normally light.
whyHigh: Logging in or out with many apps restoring windows
Apps being quit and relaunched
whatToDo: Wait a moment after login
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; window restoration may not work briefly.

processes.title: pkd
processes.oneLiner: Manages app plug-ins and extensions (PlugInKit), such as share, Finder and widget extensions.
processes.summary: pkd manages plug-ins for PlugInKit, the system macOS uses to discover and launch app extensions such as share extensions, Finder extensions and widgets. It's normally light, with brief activity when apps or extensions are installed.
whyHigh: Installing or updating apps that include extensions
Many extensions being discovered after an update
whatToDo: Wait for installs to finish
Turn off extensions you don't use in System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; extensions may briefly fail to load.

processes.title: imklaunchagent
processes.oneLiner: Launches keyboard input methods, such as Chinese, Japanese or emoji input.
processes.summary: imklaunchagent launches input methods (alternative ways of typing, like Chinese pinyin, Japanese or third-party keyboards) when you select them. Apple says it must not be terminated. It's normally idle.
whyHigh: Switching input sources often
A third-party input method misbehaving
whatToDo: Remove input sources you don't use in System Settings > Keyboard > Text Input
Update or remove third-party input methods
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: Apple says it must not be terminated; typing with input methods depends on it.

processes.title: syslogd
processes.oneLiner: The older Apple System Log server, still used by some apps and tools to record messages.
processes.summary: syslogd receives and processes log messages sent through older logging interfaces. Most of macOS now uses the unified logging system (logd), but syslogd remains for compatibility. It's normally very light.
whyHigh: An app writing lots of messages through older logging interfaces
Something failing repeatedly and logging each time
whatToDo: Look for another busy or crashing process at the same time
Update the app producing the messages
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it; some log messages may be lost.

processes.title: taskgated
processes.oneLiner: Decides whether one program may inspect or control another, such as a debugger attaching to an app.
processes.summary: taskgated implements the policy for a sensitive system service that lets one process access another's internals, which debuggers and some developer tools need. The kernel asks taskgated to approve or deny such requests. It's normally idle.
whyHigh: Debuggers or developer tools attaching to processes
Security or monitoring software inspecting processes
whatToDo: Stop debugging sessions you don't need
Restart your Mac
processes.safeToQuitNote: macOS relaunches it when needed.

processes.title: Taskyfy
processes.oneLiner: The app you're using right now: it measures your Mac and explains what it finds.
processes.summary: Taskyfy samples CPU, memory, energy and temperatures and keeps a small local history. TaskyfyHelper is its optional, read-only helper that measures macOS's own processes. Neither sends your data anywhere.
whyHigh: The main window or menu bar popover is open, so Taskyfy samples every second instead of every 5–10 seconds.
The Temperature screen is open, which reads all sensors.
whatToDo: Close the window when you don't need it; Taskyfy drops to background sampling automatically.
Check its own cost any time at the bottom of the sidebar.
processes.safeToQuitNote: Quitting simply stops monitoring; history already saved stays on your Mac.

typical.cpu: About 0.1–0.5% in the background; 1–3% with the window open

patterns.title: Browser / Electron renderer helper
patterns.oneLiner: Runs web pages or an app's interface for a Chromium browser or an Electron app.
patterns.summary: Apps built on Chromium (Chrome, Edge, Brave) or Electron (Slack, Discord, VS Code, Notion and many more) split their work into helper processes. 'Renderer' helpers run web pages or the app's own interface, usually one per site, tab, window or extension. The start of the name tells you which app it belongs to. Many of them at once is normal.
whyHigh: A heavy web page or app view: video, animation, large documents
Many tabs, windows or views open
Extensions or plug-ins running scripts
A page or view stuck in a loop
whatToDo: Look at the start of the name to see which app it belongs to
Use that app's own task manager if it has one (Chrome/Edge/Brave: Window or More tools > Task Manager)
Close the tab, window or view that's busy
Quit and reopen the app
patterns.safeToQuitNote: Quitting one closes or crashes the tab or window it was running; the rest of the app keeps going.

patterns.title: Browser / Electron GPU helper
patterns.oneLiner: Handles graphics and video for a Chromium browser or Electron app.
patterns.summary: Chromium browsers and Electron apps use one 'GPU' helper to draw their interface, play video and run graphics effects using your Mac's graphics hardware. The start of the name tells you which app it belongs to. It's busier when that app shows video or animation.
whyHigh: Video or animation playing in the app
Video calls or screen sharing
Graphics driver or hardware acceleration issues
whatToDo: Pause video or close animated content in that app
Quit and reopen the app
Look for a 'hardware acceleration' setting in the app and try toggling it
patterns.safeToQuitNote: The app usually restarts it; its window may flicker or video may stop briefly.

patterns.title: Browser / Electron plugin helper
patterns.oneLiner: A helper process that an Electron or Chromium-based app uses for plug-ins or extensions.
patterns.summary: Electron and Chromium-based apps include a 'Plugin' helper variant for code that needs extra permissions. Apps use it for different things; in code editors like VS Code and Cursor it typically runs extensions and the language tools they start. The start of the name tells you which app it belongs to.
whyHigh: Extensions or plug-ins doing heavy work
Language tools analysing a large project (in code editors)
A plug-in stuck in a loop
whatToDo: Identify the app from the start of the name
Disable extensions or plug-ins in that app one at a time
Quit and reopen the app
patterns.safeToQuitNote: Features provided by that helper stop until the app restarts it.

patterns.title: App helper process (other variant)
patterns.oneLiner: A specialised helper process belonging to a browser or Electron-based app.
patterns.summary: Chromium-based browsers and Electron apps use several kinds of helper processes, labelled in brackets, for jobs such as notifications ('Alerts') and other specialised tasks. The start of the name tells you which app it belongs to. These are a normal part of how such apps are built.
whyHigh: The app it belongs to is busy
A specific feature of the app is working hard
whatToDo: Identify the app from the start of the name
Quit and reopen that app
Update the app
patterns.safeToQuitNote: The related feature of that app may stop working until the app restarts it.

patterns.title: App helper process
patterns.oneLiner: A background helper that belongs to the app named at the start.
patterns.summary: Many apps, especially browsers and Electron apps, run work in separate '... Helper' processes for stability and security. The first part of the name is usually the app it belongs to. Seeing several helpers for one app is normal.
whyHigh: The parent app is busy (syncing, loading content, playing media)
Extensions or background features of that app
whatToDo: Identify the app from the start of the name and check what it's doing
Quit and reopen that app
Update the app
patterns.safeToQuitNote: Usually safe, but part of the parent app may stop working until it's restarted.

patterns.title: WebKit process
patterns.oneLiner: A WebKit process that shows web content for Safari or another app.
patterns.summary: WebKit is Apple's web engine, used by Safari and by any app that shows web content (Mail, the App Store and many third-party apps). It splits work into separate processes for web content, networking and graphics, for security and stability. Activity reflects what the web pages in that app are doing.
whyHigh: Heavy web pages: video, animation or web apps
Many tabs or web views open
Pages downloading lots of data
whatToDo: Close tabs or windows showing heavy pages
Quit and reopen the app that shows the web content
Restart your Mac if it stays high with no web content open
patterns.safeToQuitNote: Web content in the related app reloads or shows an error; the app itself keeps running.

patterns.title: Spotlight indexing worker
patterns.oneLiner: A Spotlight worker that reads files so they can be found in search.
patterns.summary: Processes whose names start with 'mdworker' are Spotlight's indexing workers. They read new and changed files and extract their text and details for search. Several can run at once and they quit when they're done.
whyHigh: Indexing after a macOS update, migration or new drive
Lots of new or changed files
whatToDo: Let indexing finish with the Mac plugged in
Exclude folders you never search in System Settings > Spotlight > Search Privacy
Restart your Mac if they stay busy for days
patterns.safeToQuitNote: Spotlight starts new workers as needed; quitting doesn't stop indexing.

patterns.title: Core Audio driver host
patterns.oneLiner: Runs an audio driver plug-in, often a virtual audio device from a meeting or recording app.
patterns.summary: macOS runs some audio driver plug-ins in their own 'Core Audio Driver' processes, separate from the main audio service, so a faulty driver can't take down all sound. The name in brackets shows the driver, which often belongs to a meeting, recording or audio-routing app (for example a virtual microphone or speaker).
whyHigh: The app that owns the driver is using it (a call, recording or audio routing)
A buggy or outdated third-party audio driver
whatToDo: Identify the app from the driver name in brackets
Quit that app if you're not using it
Update or uninstall audio software you no longer need
patterns.safeToQuitNote: The related audio device stops working until macOS reloads the driver.

patterns.title: Crashpad crash reporter
patterns.oneLiner: A crash reporter from a Chromium-based browser or Electron app, waiting in case of crashes.
patterns.summary: Crashpad is the crash-reporting tool used by Chromium browsers and many Electron apps. It waits quietly in the background and records a report if its app crashes. It normally uses almost no resources.
whyHigh: Its app is crashing and reports are being written
Crash reports being uploaded after a crash
whatToDo: Check the file path to see which app it belongs to
Update or reinstall that app if it keeps crashing
patterns.safeToQuitNote: Safe to quit; the app just won't record crash reports until restarted.

patterns.title: Docker Desktop component
patterns.oneLiner: A background component of Docker Desktop.
patterns.summary: Processes whose names start with 'com.docker.' belong to Docker Desktop, which runs containers inside a Linux virtual machine on your Mac. Their usage reflects what your containers are doing.
whyHigh: Containers running heavy workloads
Image builds or file sharing with large folders
whatToDo: Stop containers you don't need
Lower resource limits in Docker Desktop > Settings > Resources
Quit Docker Desktop from its menu when not in use
patterns.safeToQuitNote: Quitting components can stop Docker and its containers; quit Docker Desktop from its menu instead.

patterns.title: App updater
patterns.oneLiner: A background updater that keeps an app up to date.
patterns.summary: Many apps install a small updater that checks for new versions in the background, even when the app is closed. These are normal and important for getting security fixes. They usually run briefly and then exit or sit idle.
whyHigh: Downloading or installing an update
An update that keeps failing and retrying
whatToDo: Let the update finish
Open the related app and check for updates manually
If you've removed the app, use its uninstaller to remove leftover updaters
patterns.safeToQuitNote: Generally safe; it will run again at its next scheduled check.

patterns.title: App extension (widget or Shortcuts/Siri intents)
patterns.oneLiner: A small app extension that provides a widget, or actions and search results for Siri, Spotlight or Shortcuts.
patterns.summary: Apps, including System Settings and other Apple apps, include small extensions that run separately from the main app. Widget extensions supply widget content, and intents extensions expose actions and searchable items to Siri, Spotlight and Shortcuts. macOS starts them when needed and stops them afterwards. Seeing many of them is normal.
whyHigh: A widget refreshing its content
Spotlight, Siri or Shortcuts querying the extension
whatToDo: Wait; these usually exit on their own
Remove widgets you don't use
Restart your Mac if one stays busy
patterns.safeToQuitNote: macOS starts it again when it's needed; the related widget or action may briefly not work.

patterns.title: XPC service
patterns.oneLiner: A small helper service that an app or macOS starts on demand to do one specific job.
patterns.summary: XPC services are small, separate helper processes that apps and macOS launch to do one job, such as decoding video, rendering a preview or handling a dialog. Splitting work this way improves security and stability: if the helper crashes, the app keeps running. They're started and stopped automatically.
whyHigh: The app that uses it is doing work that relies on this service
A service stuck on a difficult task
whatToDo: Check which app you were using when it got busy
Quit and reopen that app
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
patterns.safeToQuitNote: It's usually restarted on demand; the feature it was serving may fail once.

patterns.title: Apple system component
patterns.oneLiner: A component of macOS or an Apple app, named with Apple's 'com.apple.' identifier.
patterns.summary: Names starting with 'com.apple.' are Apple's own identifiers, typically used for helper services inside macOS and Apple apps. These are normally started and stopped automatically by the system. To confirm it's genuine, check that the file lives inside /System, /usr or an Apple app.
whyHigh: The Apple feature it serves is busy
Background maintenance, often after a macOS update
whatToDo: Wait a few minutes; most activity is temporary
Check its file path to confirm it's inside /System or an Apple app
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
Install the latest macOS update
patterns.safeToQuitNote: macOS usually restarts it when needed; the related feature may stop briefly.

patterns.title: Background agent
patterns.oneLiner: A background helper that runs in your login session, for macOS or an installed app.
patterns.summary: On macOS, an 'agent' is a background process that runs in your user session, as opposed to a daemon, which runs for the whole system. Both Apple and third-party apps use agents, for things like menu bar items, sync, notifications and updates. Check its file path: Apple's agents live in /System or /usr, while app agents usually live inside the app or in a Library folder.
whyHigh: The feature or app it belongs to is busy (syncing, updating, indexing)
An agent from an app you no longer use, still running
whatToDo: Check its file path to see what it belongs to
Review System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions for third-party items
Quit and reopen the related app, or restart your Mac
patterns.safeToQuitNote: Usually safe, but it may relaunch and the related feature may stop working briefly.

patterns.title: Background service
patterns.oneLiner: A background service started by macOS or an app to handle a specific task.
patterns.summary: Processes ending in 'Service' are usually background helpers that macOS or an app starts on demand to do one kind of job. If the name starts with 'com.apple.' or the file lives in /System or /usr/libexec, it's part of macOS. Otherwise, the name or file path usually points to the app it belongs to.
whyHigh: The feature or app it serves is busy
A task it's handling is large or stuck
whatToDo: Check its file path to see whether it's part of macOS or an app
Quit and reopen the related app
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
patterns.safeToQuitNote: It's usually restarted on demand; the feature it serves may stop briefly.

patterns.title: Probably a background daemon
patterns.oneLiner: Likely a background daemon; macOS service names often end in 'd'. Check its location to be sure.
patterns.summary: By Unix tradition, background services (daemons) often have names ending in 'd', like launchd or cloudd, and macOS has hundreds of them. This is only a naming convention, so it's not a guarantee: some ordinary tools also end in 'd'. If the file lives in /System, /usr/libexec or /usr/sbin, it's part of macOS and protected by the system; elsewhere, it belongs to software you installed.
whyHigh: It's doing scheduled background work (syncing, indexing, maintenance)
Something it depends on is failing and it keeps retrying
whatToDo: Check the file path: /System, /usr/libexec and /usr/sbin are macOS locations
Wait a few minutes; many daemons work in short bursts
If it belongs to an app, update or quit that app
Restart your Mac if it stays busy
patterns.safeToQuitNote: macOS daemons usually relaunch automatically; quitting rarely helps and can interrupt a feature.
